question: When oil becomes an imperial commodity, who supplies it, who is barred from it — and where do pressing and churning begin elsewhere?
thesis: From 300 BC to 600 AD olive oil becomes an imperial commodity: a hill of 50 million jars at Rome, a Tripolitanian boom and an oil annona show a state feeding its capital on oil. In India and China the move is from ghee and animal fat to pressed seed oils, and when the western empire falls the butter and animal fat of the north come back.

big_ideas.title: Oil feeds an empire
big_ideas.text: Monte Testaccio in Rome is a man-made hill of over 50 million amphorae, mostly oil jars; Tripolitania has hundreds of presses and its elite grows rich on exports; and a rule of thumb of 20 litres a head puts the Mediterranean’s need at hundreds of millions of litres a year, though that figure is contested.

big_ideas.title: The state treats oil as public business
big_ideas.text: Ptolemy II taxes five oils, Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil for backing the wrong side, Leptis gives Rome a gift of oil that leads to an official for the oil annona, and Delos’s rents rise and fall with the price of oil.

big_ideas.title: India and China turn to pressed seed oils
big_ideas.text: Indian doctors already prefer sesame oil for frying and advise ghee only in the autumn, the Arthaśāstra prices oil in the meat shop, and the Periplus lists ghee and sesame oil as exports. In China pressing seeds begins only in the late Han and by 544 colza and hemp oil are trade goods.

big_ideas.title: Butter is the barbarian’s fat, until the north takes over
big_ideas.text: Galen says butter is for cold regions without olive oil and Greek and Roman medicine uses it only in poultices. When the Germanic peoples overrun the western empire they bring meat, beer and animal fat, and a Gallo-Roman bishop complains of a Burgundian with rancid butter on his hair.

threads.title: Rome and its oil provinces
threads.claim: The Roman oil economy grows from a Punic manual and a Greek press into a trade run by provincial elites for the capital.

beats.text: Mago of Carthage writes the farming manual in Punic that Rome later has translated.
Cato describes the beam press, and Pliny lists the screw press and the roller mill.
Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil after the civil war.
Monte Testaccio rises from over 50 million amphorae, mostly from southern Spain.
About 20 litres a head would make the Mediterranean’s need 500 to 1,000 million litres a year.
The territory of Lepcis holds perhaps 1,500 olive presses, and its elite grows rich on oil.
Tripolitanian oil reaches Rome and Ostia in its own amphorae, stamped by elite estates.
Lepcis’s gift of oil to Rome leads to a procurator for the Tripolitanian oil annona.

threads.title: The eastern Mediterranean: Delos, Egypt and the Menorah
threads.claim: East of the olive heartland the oils come from other plants, and oil is tax, rent and sacred ration.

beats.text: On Delos, farms with no olives pay rents that rise and fall with the price of oil.
Ptolemy II’s Revenue Laws tax five oils, among them castor.
The Fayum papyri name castor, linseed, radish, safflower, sesame and olive oil.
In tradition, one day’s lamp oil lights the Temple Menorah for eight days.

threads.title: India: from ghee to oil
threads.claim: Indian sources of the early centuries AD already show oil on the market, in the kitchen and in the physician’s advice.

beats.text: The Pali Vinaya lets sick monks take ghee, butter, oil, honey and syrup after midday.
The Periplus lists ghee and sesame oil among goods carried from Indian ports to the African coast.
Caraka advises ghee in autumn and sesame oil for frying; Suśruta counts sixty oilseeds.
The Arthaśāstra gives the oil, curds and spices for dressing 20 palas of meat in a shop.

threads.title: China learns to press seeds
threads.claim: China’s cooking fats are animal fats until the Han, then seed oils become a commercial trade within about five centuries.

beats.text: Tradition says Zhang Qian brings sesame from the west along the Silk Road.
Needham concludes that pressing seeds for oil was not accomplished until the late Han.
A warehouse holds ten thousand piculs of hemp oil, a record of oil as a trade commodity.
The Chhi min yao shu has colza seed sold to the oil mills, worth as much as hulled grain.
The same manual teaches how to churn su, China’s butter-like fat, from soured milk.

threads.title: The north’s fats return
threads.claim: Butter and animal fat, scorned by the Mediterranean, come back with the new rulers.

beats.text: Galen says people in cold regions without olive oil wash with butter, and that doctors use it in poultices.
The Germanic peoples bring a cuisine of meat, beer and animal fat in place of bread, wine and oil.
Sidonius Apollinaris complains of a Burgundian with his head ‘perfumed with rancid butter’.
The physician Anthimus prescribes fresh unsalted butter with honey for consumption.

turning_points.text: Ptolemy II taxes five oils in Egypt.
Mago’s Punic farming manual is written.
Cato describes the beam press for olives.
Sesame is said to reach China.
Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil.
The Periplus lists Indian ghee and sesame oil as exports.
Monte Testaccio grows to over 50 million jars.
China learns to press oil from seeds.
Indian medicine prefers sesame oil to ghee for frying.
Rome appoints an official for Tripolitania’s oil annona.
The Germanic peoples bring animal fat to the western empire.
The Chhi min yao shu records colza oil mills.

text: Rome as consumer and administrator: the jars of Monte Testaccio, the per-head figure, the beam and screw presses, soap as a cosmetic, Gaul’s butter, Galen and Anthimus on butter, Delos’s rents and the Germanic shift ([[ec1]], [[ec3]], [[te1]], [[te3]], [[e1]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[ec6]], [[w1]]).

Three entries: Ptolemy II’s tax on five oils in Egypt, the oils named in the Greek papyri of the Fayum, and the Hanukkah lamp-oil legend ([[o1]], [[ec8]], [[b2]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy, though the Tripolitanian and Punic oils are North African.

India and China each begin their own fat story: the Buddha’s five medicines, Caraka on ghee, the Arthaśāstra shop, the Periplus’s exports; China learns to press seeds and churn su, and sesame arrives by the Silk Road ([[b1]], [[th3]], [[ec5]], [[x3]], [[te2]], [[te4]], [[th4]], [[ec4]], [[x2]]).

Carthage and Tripolitania: Mago’s manual, Caesar’s fine on Leptis, the oil gift to Rome, the olive boom and Tripolitanian oil in Rome ([[th5]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[ec2]], [[x1]]). All five entries are the Roman province seen from Rome. Sub-Saharan Africa has no entry; the shea record begins in the next folio.
No entry. Nothing in the library bears on American fats in these centuries.
One entry: the domesticated coconut carried by Polynesians, whose ancestral culture emerged in Tonga and Samoa in the second half of the first millennium BC ([[ec7]]).

sources.intro: A scholarly archaeology of Roman oil in Mattingly, a scholarly translation of Chinese farm and oil texts in Needham, popular histories for butter, and Achaya for India.
main: Mattingly, *Tripolitania* and ‘The Olive Boom’, for the Libyan estates, amphorae and annona ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[x1]], [[ec3]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for the Chinese presses, oils and su ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec4]], [[th4]], [[te4]]).
Achaya for India ([[th3]], [[ec5]], [[x3]]); Khosrova and Mueller for Rome's butter and the Germanic shift ([[th1]], [[th2]], [[e1]], [[w1]]); Dalby for Egypt ([[o1]]).
Foxhall for Delos ([[ec6]]); Mueller for Hanukkah ([[b2]]); encyclopedia and lecture notes found by search for Mago ([[th5]]); Kiple for the coconut ([[ec7]]).
Lucas, read from a scanned copy, for Egypt’s oils in the Greek papyri ([[ec8]]).
contested: Whether Caesar's fine was annual and which Leptis it fell on ([[o2]]); the Arthaśāstra's date ([[ec5]]).
The first pressing of oil in China is an argument from absence ([[te2]]).
The Germanic ‘revenge of animal fat’ is Mueller's interpretation ([[w1]]).
Dating of the Monte Testaccio dump is the folio's, not a cited figure ([[ec1]]).
Mago’s date is unsettled ([[th5]]); Mueller dates the Hanukkah miracle to 168 BC, where 164 BC is the usual year ([[b2]]); the coconut entry’s date is a placeholder ([[ec7]]).
gaps: Roman literary sources (Cato, Columella, Pliny) were not read directly; nor the Egyptian papyri.
Soap in antiquity rests on two passing mentions ([[te3]]).
Sub-Saharan Africa has no entry in this folio; the shea sequence at Kirikongo starts about 100 AD and is filed in the next folio ([[ec7]] in fats-600-1000).

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.
The Roman entries sit in *Economy*, *Order* and *Technology*; the Indian and Chinese ones in *Thought*. Read the Nexus for the Tripolitanian chain from estates to jars to Rome.
Note the numbers: they are Mattingly's and Foxhall's estimates, not Roman records, and their tier labels say so.

The *picture by region* counts the 27 entries: Europe 9, Near East 3, Far East 9, Africa 5, Oceania 1; none in Americas or Worldwide. Africa here is the Roman oil province seen from Rome, not the home of African fats.
